content: Chronic mountain sickness (CMS), also referred to as Monge's disease, was first described in 1925 by Carlos Monge. High Altitude Flatus Expulsion was initially documented by Joseph Hamel around 1820 and later rediscovered in 1981 by Paul Auerbach and York Miller. Altitude sickness can be categorized into two groups based on clinical symptoms and pathological changes in affected organs: acute and chronic. The condition arises due to increased pulmonary artery pressure caused by hypoxia-induced pulmonary vasoconstriction. Hypoxia triggers physiological adaptations such as increased oxygen delivery to tissues, enhanced ventilation, elevated cardiac output, and higher hemoglobin concentrations. These changes improve ventilation-perfusion matching and gas exchange but can lead to high-altitude pulmonary hypertension. The primary cause of altitude sickness is the combination of reduced air pressure and lower oxygen concentration at high altitudes. Risk factors include pre-existing lung disease, conditions or substances that impair acclimatization, a history of altitude sickness, and inadequate acclimatization. Routine screening for altitude sickness, such as cold pressor tests, heart rate variability, or pulmonary function tests, is not supported by sufficient evidence. The most significant complications of altitude sickness are high-altitude pulmonary edema (HAPE) and cerebral edema. The prognosis is generally favorable, with a five-year mortality rate of approximately 12% for affected patients. Patients with altitude sickness often have a history of underlying lung disease or factors that interfere with acclimatization. Common symptoms include headache, dizziness, fatigue, and cyanosis. Physical examination findings typically include headache, nausea, vomiting, and lightheadedness. Laboratory findings consistent with altitude sickness include elevated hemoglobin, hematocrit, and blood urea nitrogen levels, along with decreased bicarbonate, creatinine, and PCO2 levels. Electrocardiogram (ECG) findings may show a shortened R-R interval, QT interval changes, ST-T flattening, and increased P wave amplitude. Chest X-rays may reveal patchy alveolar infiltrates, predominantly in the right central hemithorax, and asymmetric airspace consolidation. CT scans can also demonstrate these findings, particularly in cases of pulmonary edema. MRI may show increased T2 signal in the white matter of the splenium of the corpus callosum. Pharmacologic treatments for altitude sickness include acetazolamide and dexamethasone. For nausea and vomiting, medications such as promethazine and ondansetron are effective. Surgical intervention is not recommended for managing altitude sickness. Primary prevention strategies include avoiding alcohol consumption, maintaining a high-carbohydrate diet, ensuring adequate hydration, limiting vigorous exertion during the initial days at high altitude, and using oxygen enrichment. There are no established measures for secondary prevention of altitude sickness. To better understand susceptibility to high-altitude pulmonary edema (HAPE), the International HAPE Database was established in 2004. Individuals with a history of HAPE can register confidentially to aid researchers in studying the condition.
